title: Detect Unauthorized Access to Cloud Secrets Management Stores
shortTitle: Detect Unauthorized Access to Cloud Secrets Management St...
summary: Cloud secrets management stores hold the credentials that everything else in an account trusts, so unauthorized access to them (T1555.006) is usually the pivot from a single compromised workload to full account takeover. This detection strategy watches control plane audit records for read operations against secret stores and the key management service calls that decrypt them, then scores each read by identity, source address, user agent, and volume. The decisive signals are an identity reading secrets it has never touched before, one identity sweeping many secrets in a short window, reads from an unusual network location or automation platform, or a secret fetched and then used from a different address minutes later. It fails most often because automation legitimately reads secrets constantly, because fine grained data plane logging is often disabled or sampled, and because shared roles make several distinct workloads look like one identity.

beginner.definition: A secrets store keeps passwords, keys, and tokens safe in the cloud. Applications read their credentials from it instead of storing them in code. This detection looks for someone reading those secrets without a good reason. It catches theft of the keys that open other systems.
beginner.whyItMatters: One stolen secret can open many systems at once. The secret may belong to a database, a payment service, or another cloud account. Because the store is designed to be read, a thief does not need to break anything. They only need permission that is too wide or a stolen identity. This detection helps you notice the theft while it happens.
howItWorks: The cloud provider writes an audit record for each call to the secrets store.
The record shows who called, from which address, and with which tool.
The rule builds a baseline of which identity normally reads which secret.
It then flags first time reads and sudden bursts of many different secrets.
It links the read to any later use of that secret from a new address.
An analyst checks the identity owner and the calling application before acting.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel with a locked cabinet of master keys. Staff open the cabinet whenever a guest is locked out. That is normal and useful. A thief who wants the whole building does not break the cabinet. They copy a staff member's badge and open it once. Nobody notices a single opening, because staff open it all day. This detection is the log book beside the cabinet. It records who opened it, when, and how many keys they took. One badge taking thirty keys at three in the morning stands out at once.
takeaways: Secrets are the highest value target in a cloud account, because they unlock everything else.
Record every read, and compare each one with what that identity normally does.
A burst of secret reads by one identity is a strong sign of theft.

objectives: Explain why secrets management stores are a priority target during cloud intrusion.
Identify the control plane audit records that capture secret read operations.
Build an identity baseline so that first time and burst reads are visible.
Correlate a secret read with later use of that secret from a new source.
Choose containment steps when a secret is suspected of being stolen.
dataSources: AWS CloudTrail management events for secrets manager and parameter store read operations including caller identity and user agent
Cloud key management audit records for decrypt calls against the keys that protect stored secrets
Azure Activity Log and key vault diagnostic logs for secret read operations with caller identity and source address
GCP Cloud Audit Logs for secret manager version access calls including principal and caller IP
logic: The pattern is unauthorized or unexpected read access to a secrets store, expressed as a deviation from the normal relationship between an identity and the secrets it uses. A detection should score each read on four axes: whether this principal has read this secret before, how many distinct secrets the principal read inside a short window, whether the caller address, user agent, or network path is new for that principal, and whether a secret retrieved by one principal is subsequently used by a different principal or from a different address. High value correlations are principal identity, secret resource name, source IP address, user agent string, and the timestamp of the read. Automation that reads one or two secrets from a stable address on a schedule is the benign case, and it dominates the volume, which is why a simple alert on any secret read is useless. The malicious case is breadth, novelty, or a read outside the hours and networks that identity has ever used before.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Burst of secret reads by a single cloud identity
# logsource:
#   product: aws
# detection:
#   selection:
#     eventSource: 'secretsmanager.amazonaws.com'
#     eventName:
#       - 'GetSecretValue'
#       - 'BatchGetSecretValue'
#   filter_known:
#     userAgent|contains: 'terraform'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known | count() by userIdentity.arn > 10
# level: high
falsePositives: Deployment pipelines that read a large bundle of application secrets during a scheduled release window
A newly onboarded application whose service role legitimately reads its own secrets for the first time
Incident response automation that rotates credentials and therefore reads every affected secret in one run
A team moving workloads between regions so the same identity appears briefly from a new address range
tuningNotes: Start by baselining the normal pairs of identity and secret, and the source addresses each identity uses, then alert on novelty and breadth rather than on raw read counts. Add filters for the user agents of your approved deployment platforms, but keep an unfiltered high severity path for reads against secrets that guard production databases or cross account trust. Scope the rule to identities outside a small allow list of infrastructure roles, and enable data plane logging on the stores that matter so the rule has events to read. Narrowing this way will miss an attacker who steals the credentials and user agent of an approved pipeline, so alert separately on any secret read followed by a use from a new source address.
